profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in an ML research lab about a two-week prototype for an internal replication-and-extension of the scikit-learn API design paper. The team wants to prepare a short demo and technical note for a lab review showing how a unified estimator API affects composition, reproducibility, and the ease of swapping models in modern Python workflows. The agenda is to decide what the first prototype should include, how 'lightweight' the implementation should be, what counts as the standard scikit-learn baselines for the examples, how the composition demo will be produced, who owns each piece, and what 'ready for the review' means in practice. The expected outcome is a concrete plan with responsibilities, a timeline for a first runnable prototype, and a shared-seeming understanding of the artifacts to bring to the lab review.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: ML systems research, experimental methodology, and research communication
members.background: Lena leads a university ML infrastructure lab and has supervised several studies on usability and reproducibility in Python ML tooling; she tends to evaluate software papers in terms of whether the implementation supports a crisp research narrative and a convincing demo.
members.private_state: She wants a polished, low-overhead prototype that can be shown confidently at the lab review without the project turning into a framework-building exercise, and she is quietly worried that engineering ambition will consume the two-week window.
hidden_assumptions: When a prototype is described as 'lightweight,' it should rely on the simplest path that produces credible evidence, typically one or two notebooks plus thin helper code rather than reusable infrastructure.
The phrase 'standard scikit-learn baselines' naturally refers to the handful of canonical estimators most readers immediately recognize for tabular ML, not coverage across sklearn subpackages.
A composition demo meant for a note or talk is primarily a didactic artifact and does not need to be generated from the same execution path as the benchmark runs.
If something must be 'ready for the review,' the outputs and narrative should be effectively frozen by the prior afternoon so slides can be assembled calmly.
Any packaging, config system, or CLI work beyond what is needed for the review is optional and should be deferred unless explicitly justified.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Python ML tooling, experiment infrastructure, benchmarking pipelines, and reproducible research workflows
members.background: Arjun previously worked on open-source evaluation tooling and joined the lab to improve how research prototypes are executed and reused; he habitually interprets even small studies through the lens of rerunnability and extension by other team members.
members.private_state: He wants to use the project to establish a reusable evaluation pattern for future papers, and he is concerned that a manually assembled demo will leave unclear provenance and force the team to redo work later.
hidden_assumptions: If an implementation is called 'lightweight,' that rules out heavy orchestration but still includes a minimal standardized runner, config files, and result logging so the work is reproducible by someone other than the author.

The phrase 'standard scikit-learn baselines' means a compact representative panel that exercises the common estimator contract across major modules such as linear models, trees, SVMs, clustering, and at least one pipeline/meta-estimator case.
A composition demo is strongest when it is emitted from the same runnable path as the rest of the experiments, so notebooks and plots are views over a single execution workflow.
If deliverables are 'ready for the review,' the essential pipeline is validated and the last clean run can happen close to the meeting if needed.
Using a small amount of structure now, such as a minimal config-driven runner, is still consistent with a research prototype and does not count as over-engineering.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to keep the prototype 'lightweight.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means lightweight as in the least-built artifact that can support the story for the review: likely a procedural notebook or two, shared helper functions, and maybe one simple script.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means lightweight as in not a full platform, but still a minimal config-driven runner with logging and a stable directory structure so others can rerun it without editing notebooks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as arguing against unnecessary complexity, so 'lightweight' feels like a clear shared value rather than a term needing unpacking; the disagreement is about the lower bound of acceptable structure, which usually remains implicit.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to start from 'the standard scikit-learn baselines.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 hears this as the few emblematic models that most readers associate with scikit-learn API examples, such as LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier, and maybe KMeans for an unsupervised contrast.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 hears this as a representative baseline panel covering the estimator interface across major sklearn families, for example LogisticRegression, LinearSVC or SVC, RandomForestClassifier, KMeans, StandardScaler plus Pipeline, and a GridSearchCV case.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds conventional and domain-familiar, and both parties believe they are advocating a modest starting point; because neither is proposing an obviously broad sweep, the difference in what counts as 'standard' stays hidden.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of ready for the review
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the prototype and results should be 'ready for the review' in two weeks.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1's criterion is that plots, tables, and the worked example are stable by the afternoon before the review, with no expectation of substantive reruns afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2's criterion is that the pipeline and artifacts are reliable enough that final runs can still happen shortly before the review if he needs to regenerate outputs from the validated setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase denotes a shared deadline and competence rather than an explicit acceptance test, so both assume the other means roughly the same thing; the real divergence is in what threshold of stability counts as 'ready,' which seldom gets stated unless a problem arises.

misalignment_points.topic: How the composition demo is supposed to be produced
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include 'a composition demo' showing pipelines and model selection.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this will be a deliberately crafted notebook walkthrough, with the pipeline and GridSearchCV example arranged pedagogically for screenshots and narrative flow in the technical note.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the same demo content will be generated from the common experiment runner, with the notebook or figures serving as a presentation layer over one reproducible execution path.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They genuinely agree on the conceptual example and even on its ingredients, so the implementation path feels like a routine execution detail; each assumes their preferred method is the obvious default for competent work.

turns.inner_thought: Two weeks is tight. I need a compact replication-and-extension that tells a clean story and does not drift into building research infrastructure. If this is going to be ready for the review, I want the figures, table, and worked example effectively settled by the prior afternoon so I can assemble slides without last-minute reruns.

I want us to treat this as a compact replication-and-extension of the scikit-learn API paper, with a prototype plan we can confidently show at the lab review in two weeks. The key thing is that the prototype and results are ready for the review and that the short demo and note tell a very clear story.

turns.inner_thought: Good framing. I can keep this lightweight without making it ad hoc: a small runner, configs, logging, and a predictable structure would still be minimal. If I set it up that way now, the lab can reuse the pattern later instead of redoing everything from scratch.
turns.utterance: That sounds right. I think we should aim for a lightweight first version that runs a few representative workflows cleanly and gives us enough material for the note.

turns.inner_thought: Starting from the standard scikit-learn baselines gives me a representative panel across familiar estimator families, including at least one case that exercises composition. That should make the setup useful beyond this single review while still looking modest.
